title: Spike forensics: WAF signature crafting and exit strategy
content:
Context / goal:
This is a working note for the SRE oncall playtest we ran 2025-10-27 simulating a credential-led traffic spike and opaque probing that slips past default rate caps. The objective: practice fast forensic triage, craft temporary WAF signatures that reduce noise without blocking legitimate clients, and define a clean exit/rollback strategy so we avoid long-lived false positives.

High-level constraints and principles (opinionated):
- Temporary mitigations must be reversible in <15m without config drift.
- Prioritize containment over perfection: if traffic is drowning production, take a broader but safe block; iterate to narrow.
- Maintain observable signals (don’t fully blackhole sources until we've recorded request context).
- Prefer allowlist exceptions for tiered customers; prefer rate-suppress routes for anonymous traffic.

Playtest summary (what happened):
- 10:07 UTC: spike started, 10k rps on text-generation endpoint region-us-west-2.
- 10:08-10:12: built-in token rate limits tripped; dataplane autoscaler attempted to add workers but queue latencies rose.
- 10:10: SRE paging triggered for API error budget drop.
- 10:12: initial triage showed ~92% of requests coming from a rotating set of IPs but identical payload prefixes (prompt header with tracking token) suggesting credential stuffing / leaked key replay.
- 10:14: first WAF safelist/deny rule deployed at edge (blocking IP CIDR ranges) — caused collateral impact on 3 paying customers. Rolled back at 10:27.

Forensics steps (checklist, order of operations):
1) Snapshot live traces and preserve logs
   - capture request logs for 10:00-10:20 window (save to s3://infra-sre/evidence/spike-20251027/).
   - run the following queries (examples):
     - unique_ips = select count(distinct origin_ip) where request_time between X and Y and path like '/v1/generate'
     - top_prefixes = group by substring(body,1,50) order by count desc limit 25
     - token_reuse = find(api_key hashed, count>10)
   - preserve KV cache metrics and eviction patterns (KV-cache-hit-rate, per-host)
2) Identify signal-bearing dimensions (these are usually the fastest to craft rules against)
   - repeated request body prefix (first ~40 bytes)
   - recurring user-agent strings or lack thereof (empty UA is often a signature)
   - header patterns (X-Client-Version, X-Forwarded-For sequences)
   - TLS client fingerprints (JA3) if available
3) Correlate with business impact
   - map affected client keys to accounts (alert product/CS for customers impacted)
   - check dedicated/dedicated-reserved pools for anomalous queue growth to identify noisy tenants

WAF signature crafting playbook (rapid, incremental approach):
- Step A: Create a detection-only signature (block=false, log=true) that matches the strongest single signal (e.g., exact 1st-40-byte prompt prefix + UA empty)
  - Rationale: verify hit-rate and false-positive risk before blocking.
  - Metric: hits/sec for signature, unique client_accounts hit.
- Step B: If signature hit-rate > 800 rps and <1% overlap with paying accounts, promote to soft-block (reject but with HTTP 429 and JSON explaining temporary throttling).
  - Soft-block allows clients to see explicit throttling and gives good UX for legitimate SDKs that implement backoff.
- Step C: If soft-block reduces traffic sufficiently and false positives remain low, convert to full deny at edge and add a short TTL on the deny rule (e.g., 4 hours), with automated rollback state.
  - Record who approved the promotion (audit trail).

Example WAF signature examples (do not use verbatim in prod, test first):
- Detection-only: match: body_prefix=="\u003cSTART_PROMPT:track=XYZ123" AND user_agent=="" -> log=true, block=false
- Soft-block: match: body_prefix in top50_prefixes AND (ja3_fingerprint in [abc123, def456] OR user_agent=="") -> return 429 with Retry-After header
- Edge deny (last resort): match: ip in dynamic_cidr_list AND body_prefix in attack_prefix_list -> block=true, ttl=4h

Rollout, approvals, and rollback policies:
- All blocking rules MUST note: author, approver, start_time, ttl, reason, hit_threshold that triggered promotion.
- Automated rollback: if customer_error_rate (5xx for dedicated customers) > 0.5% or if number_of_unique_customer_ids_blocked > 1 in the first 30 minutes, immediately rollback.
- Manual rollback: pager owner can rollback earlier if urgent.

Exit strategy / post-containment cleanup (so we don't leave band-aids):
1) After traffic falls under baseline + buffer for 60 minutes, disable deny rules and keep detection-only signatures for 24–72 hours to gather evidence.
2) Convert effective detection signatures into permanent monitoring rules (not denies) and file follow-up tickets for product/edge to evaluate long-term mitigations (quota per API-key, improved KMS rotation guidance, SDK hardening).
3) For any impacted paying customer, open a post-incident CS case and provide timeline + request logs + steps taken.
4) Archive preserved logs and a summary into the incident Jira and Confluence pages.

Playtest observations (lessons from the 10/27 run):
- We rolled a CIDR deny too early; impact: 3 paying customers effected. Cause: coarse IP provisioning by a major mobile CDN.
- Detection-only signatures gave a reliable hit-count quickly and were invaluable for estimating FP risk.
- Edge deny TTL automation didn't exist: operator manually tracked expires on a Google doc -> automate TTL in WAF config next time.
- We lacked an easy way to map hashed API keys in logs back to customer ids without hitting support database; add a read-only mapping cache in the SRE toolkit.

Suggested additions to infra / tech debt to reduce future blast radius:
- WAF: ability to attach expiry and automated rollbacks to deny rules with safe default of 4h and human approval to extend.
- Observability: pre-built forensics dashboards for spikes: top prefixes, top UAs, top hashed-api-keys, ja3 fingerprints, top CIDRs, and per-route latency.
- Automation: a safe "soft-block promotion" flow in a CLI so oncall can promote detection->soft-block->deny with one command and required confirmation prompts.
- Playbooks: standard templates for customer communications when customers are impacted by mitigations.

Unresolved questions / discussion items:
- Should we allow TTLs longer than 24 hours for denies in extreme abuse? (tradeoff: easier containment vs. long-lived false positives)
- Can we centralize a read-only api-key->customer mapping accessible to oncall without exposing keys? (proposal: hashed-key mapping + short TTL caching).
- How to better integrate Dedicated pool telemetry into the early-warning system so we can isolate noisy tenants earlier?

Immediate action items (owners & rough ETA):
- E2E: add deny TTL field + auto-rollback rule to WAF config schema (owner: Marcus Chen, ETA: 2026-03-01).
- Observability: build spike forensic dashboard template (owner: Priya Singh, ETA: 2026-01-12).
- SRE toolkit: add mapping cache for api-key->customer id (owner: Ethan Morales, ETA: 2026-02-01).
- Docs: convert this playtest note into a short runbook with CLI commands and checklists (owner: Samira Lopez, ETA: 2025-11-15).

Quick-reference checklist for oncall (one-pager):
- preserve logs -> snapshot traces -> s3 store
- quick queries: top prefixes, top IPs, ja3, UA, hashed-key reuse
- deploy detection-only signature; monitor 5–10 minutes
- promote to soft-block if clear (>800 rps unique non-customer)
- if soft-block works and FP low -> edge deny with ttl (4h) and audit metadata
- prepare rollback if customer errors or CS reports impact

Appendix: forensic query snippets (examples to drop into Kibana / Athena / Datadog)
- top prefixes: SELECT substring(body,1,60) as prefix, count(*) as c FROM requests WHERE path LIKE '/v1/%' AND timestamp BETWEEN X AND Y GROUP BY prefix ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 50;
- hashed-key reuse: SELECT api_key_hash, count(distinct origin_ip) FROM requests WHERE timestamp BETWEEN X AND Y GROUP BY api_key_hash HAVING count(*)>50;
- candidate-ja3: SELECT ja3, count(*) FROM requests WHERE timestamp BETWEEN X AND Y GROUP BY ja3 ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT 50;

Notes to self: keep the playtest simple next time — simulate a rotating-IP leak with two different prompt families so we exercise signature-narrowing and see collateral. Also test TTL automation end-to-end in staging WAF before using in prod.
